strengths: Significance: Reliable abstention for pairwise LLM judging is a useful problem, with clear applications to benchmarking and preference labeling. Optimizing coverage subject to an explicit error budget is a practical objective.

Empirical merits: Bidirectional aggregation improves accuracy and uncertainty discrimination across multiple benchmarks and judge sizes. For example, Table 1 reports Qwen-14B MT-Bench AUROC increasing from 0.704 to 0.777 and Qwen-7B RewardBench accuracy increasing from 0.757 to 0.807.

Presentation and reproducibility: The method is simple to understand, and the appendix provides prompts, scoring equations, baseline configurations, hardware, and the repeated calibration/test split protocol.

Limitations and ethics: Section 6 appropriately acknowledges distribution shift, logit-access requirements, computational overhead, binary-only evaluation, and residual biases. These are useful qualifications; no distinct material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—decisive: Theorem 2.1 is false under its stated assumptions. Consider a constant uncertainty score, independent identically distributed errors with probability 0.2, n = 10, and alpha = 0.1. Equation 5 is feasible exactly when all ten calibration predictions are correct, an event with probability 0.8^10; the rule then accepts every test example and otherwise abstains. Consequently, the ratio in Equation 7 equals (0.2 × 0.8^10)/(0.8^10) = 0.2, exceeding alpha. In Appendix A, Equation 13 incorrectly invokes exchangeability to equate test loss with the average calibration-plus-test loss at a threshold fitted only to calibration data. Exchangeability of the observations does not establish this equality. The central finite-sample guarantee therefore requires a substantially different argument or procedure.

Experimental consistency: Some reported accuracy, coverage, and risk results appear incompatible under the stated common prediction protocol. Table 1 gives Qwen-7B BPE accuracy 0.738 on MT-Bench, while Figure 2 reports coverage 0.991 at alpha = 0.25. Rejecting approximately 0.009 of examples cannot remove enough of the approximately 0.262 total error mass to obtain the below-0.25 risk claimed in Figure 3. Even the lower bound obtained by assuming every rejected example is erroneous leaves approximately 0.253 error mass. The manuscript should reconcile these numbers and provide the underlying predictions and split-level results.

Evaluation of the guarantee: Equation 7 targets a ratio of expectations over calibration and test randomness, whereas the experimental protocol describes averaging per-split error ratios. These quantities generally differ when coverage varies. Neither an average below alpha nor the plotted standard deviations establish a per-calibration-set guarantee. The paper needs to distinguish its statistical target from conventional expected false-discovery proportion and report a matching estimator.

Attribution and comparative evidence: Table 3 changes both the scoring/prediction method and the calibration rule: heuristic and naive baselines use unidirectional predictive probability, while SCOPE uses BPE. Thus, coverage gains do not isolate the contribution of the finite-sample correction. Essential comparisons include naive calibration using BPE, the proposed calibration using unidirectional scores, and established valid risk-control procedures using the same BPE scores. The introduction criticizes conservative alternatives without experimentally comparing against them.

Originality: The contribution beyond existing components is limited as currently established. Position swapping is acknowledged prior practice, and binary entropy is a monotone transformation of max(p̄, 1−p̄), so it introduces no distinct selection ranking beyond confidence in the averaged prediction. The calibration construction is explicitly adapted from prior linear-expectation work. A useful application contribution remains possible, but stronger controlled evidence is needed once the unsupported guarantee is removed.

Reproducibility and claim precision: Dataset versions, sampled instance identifiers, actual seeds, and executable calibration code are not supplied. Appendix B.3.2 also extracts first-token A/B logits while the prompt requests [[A]]/[[B]], leaving unclear whether logits are measured at the actual verdict position. Finally, Section 4.1's claim that BPE improves ECE over verbalized confidence in most configurations contradicts Table 1, where verbalized confidence has lower ECE in eight of twelve settings. These issues need clarification before the empirical conclusions can be reliably reproduced.

strengths: Significance: Reliable abstention for pairwise LLM judging is a useful problem. The evaluation spans three benchmarks and four judge sizes, providing evidence beyond a single model or dataset.

Empirical merit: Bidirectional probability averaging consistently improves accuracy and AUROC over unidirectional predictive probability in Table 1. For Qwen-14B on MT-Bench, AUROC increases from 0.704 to 0.777.

Presentation and limitations: The method is straightforward to understand, and the appendix provides prompts, scoring details, and hardware information. Section 6 appropriately acknowledges exchangeability, logit access, computational overhead, and remaining biases. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness, decisive: Theorem 2.1 is false under its stated assumptions. Consider i.i.d. examples with a constant uncertainty score and independent error probability 0.2, with n=10 and alpha=0.1. Equation 5 permits accepting everything exactly when all calibration predictions are correct; otherwise the method abstains everywhere. Acceptance therefore has positive probability, but the independent test error conditional on acceptance remains 0.2, violating Equation 7. Appendix A, Equation 13 incorrectly invokes exchangeability: a threshold fitted on the first n observations does not treat calibration and test observations symmetrically. The claimed finite-sample guarantee requires a substantive reformulation, not merely a clearer proof.

Evaluation of the guarantee: The theorem targets a ratio of expectations over calibration and test randomness, whereas the experiments average split-specific error ratios. These are different quantities when coverage varies. Neither mean curves below alpha nor 1,000 repeated splits establish the stated guarantee, and the manuscript sometimes describes marginal control as though it ensured reliability for each deployed calibration.

Attribution and comparisons: Table 3 changes both the uncertainty/prediction mechanism and the calibration procedure: heuristic and naive baselines use unidirectional predictive probabilities, whereas SCOPE uses BPE. Consequently, the coverage improvements do not isolate the benefit of the proposed calibration. Missing comparisons include naive calibration using BPE and established valid risk-control methods using the same BPE predictions, despite claims that existing methods are overly conservative.

Originality: The calibration construction explicitly follows prior linear expectation constraints, while response swapping is acknowledged prior practice. Binary entropy is monotone in max(p, 1-p), so the entropy transformation adds no new selection ranking beyond averaged-probability confidence. The manuscript needs stronger evidence of a distinct contribution beyond combining these ingredients.

Reproducibility: Appendix B instructs models to output [[A]] or [[B]] but extracts A/B logits at the first response token. Without specifying a supplied prefix or the actual verdict-token position, those logits need not represent the requested verdict probabilities. Exact dataset versions, sampled instance identifiers, and split seeds are also not supplied, limiting independent verification.

Presentation and claim calibration: Section 4.1 claims better ECE than verbalized confidence across most configurations, but Table 1 supports this in only 5 of 12 settings. Permutation invariance establishes order symmetry, not general freedom from bias. These overstatements matter because the broader reliability claims already depend on an invalid theorem.

strengths: Significance: Controlling errors among accepted LLM judgments is a useful objective for automated evaluation. Pairing selective prediction with an uncertainty signal designed for response-order sensitivity is practically motivated.

Empirical merits: Evaluation covers three benchmarks and four judge models. Table 1 reports consistently better discrimination for BPE than single-order predictive probability; for example, Qwen-14B AUROC on MT-Bench increases from 0.704 to 0.777. Comparisons with simulated annotators provide additional evidence that bidirectional aggregation is a useful confidence signal.

Presentation and reproducibility: The main pipeline is understandable, and the appendix supplies prompt templates, probability aggregation, metric definitions, hardware, and calibration/test proportions.

Limitations and ethics: Section 6 appropriately acknowledges exchangeability, logit access, inference overhead, binary judgments, and remaining biases. These are useful disclosures, and the manuscript presents no apparent material research-ethics concern.
weaknesses: Soundness—decisive: Theorem 2.1 is false under its stated assumptions. In Appendix A, Eq. 13 treats calibration and test losses evaluated at a calibration-dependent threshold as exchangeable. The threshold depends on calibration labels but not the test label, so this equality does not follow. A concrete counterexample uses constant uncertainty scores, independent Bernoulli(0.2) prediction errors, n = 10, and alpha = 0.1. Equation 5 permits acceptance exactly when all ten calibration predictions are correct; otherwise the method abstains. Acceptance therefore occurs with probability 0.8^10, while the independent test error remains 0.2. Consequently, E[error × selection]/E[selection] = 0.2 > 0.1. This directly contradicts the central finite-sample guarantee, even with i.i.d. data.

Evaluation does not establish the stated guarantee: Theorem 2.1 targets a ratio of joint expectations over calibration and test randomness, whereas the experimental protocol describes averaging per-split empirical error ratios. These generally differ when coverage varies. Neither quantity guarantees that each deployed calibration threshold or realized test batch stays below alpha. Statements that empirical risk must consistently remain below alpha overstate even the intended marginal guarantee.

Comparisons confound the calibration method with the prediction and uncertainty signal. The heuristic and naive baselines use single-order predictive probability, while SCOPE uses BPE, which also changes predictions. Table 3 therefore cannot isolate the benefit of the finite-sample correction or substantiate the claimed coverage advantage of SCOPE itself. Necessary comparisons include naive calibration with BPE and established valid risk-control procedures with the same BPE predictions and scores; the conservative methods criticized in the introduction are not evaluated.

Originality is limited as currently established. Bidirectional averaging builds on acknowledged position-swapping approaches, while the calibration constraint is adapted from LEC. Binary entropy is a monotone transformation of max(average preference probability, 1 − average preference probability), so it introduces no new selection ranking beyond aggregated confidence. The useful empirical adaptation could constitute a contribution, but stronger ablations or new understanding are needed, especially because the claimed theoretical contribution fails.

Some presentation claims exceed the evidence. Section 4.1 claims lower ECE than both predictive probability and verbalized confidence across most configurations, but verbalized confidence has lower ECE than BPE in eight of twelve Table 1 settings. Permutation invariance also does not establish that the resulting probabilities are generally 'bias-neutral,' although Section 6 appropriately acknowledges residual biases.

Reproducibility remains incomplete in consequential places. Appendix B.3.2 describes extracting A/B logits at the first response token despite prompting for bracketed outputs such as [[A]]; the exact decoding position and prefix handling need clarification. Exact dataset versions, sampled instance identifiers, seed values, and executable calibration code are also needed to audit the unusually tight reported risk values and resolve the theoretical discrepancy.

strengths: Significance: Selective LLM judging addresses a useful practical problem: trading evaluation coverage against disagreement with reference preferences. A lightweight method requiring two judge passes and no retraining could be valuable.

Empirical merits: Table 1 reports consistent improvements over discrete Swap-and-Aggregate in uncertainty ranking and calibration across four judges and three benchmarks. The specialized-critic experiments and calibration-size ablations broaden the evaluation.

Presentation and limitations: The framework is clearly organized, with explicit equations, prompts, and implementation details. Section 6 appropriately acknowledges exchangeability, logit access, and computational requirements; Appendix H usefully demonstrates failures under distribution shift. These disclosed limitations are informative rather than grounds for rejection.
weaknesses: Soundness—decisive: Theorem 2.1 is false under its stated assumptions. Consider constant uncertainty scores, independent Bernoulli errors with probability 0.20, n = 10, and alpha = 0.10. Equation 5 is feasible exactly when all calibration predictions are correct, an event with probability 0.8^10; Equation 6 then accepts every test example and otherwise abstains everywhere. Consequently, E[ES]/E[S] = 0.20, exceeding alpha despite i.i.d. data. Appendix A, Equation 13 incorrectly treats losses on calibration and test examples as exchangeable at the same calibration-fitted threshold. Symmetry within the calibration set does not justify this identity. This invalidates the central finite-sample reliability claim.

Risk evaluation does not match the theorem's estimand. The experiments average per-split accepted-set error rates, whereas Equation 7 specifies a ratio of expectations over calibration and test randomness. These generally differ when coverage varies. The handling of splits with zero accepted examples is also unspecified and is particularly consequential for JudgeBench, where Table 5 reports coverage of 0.023 with standard deviation 0.041. Mean empirical curves below alpha cannot establish the claimed distribution-free guarantee or guarantee safety for an individual deployment.

Comparative evidence does not isolate the calibration contribution. Table 3 uses predictive probability for the heuristic and naive baselines but bidirectional predictions and BPE for SCOPE, changing both the predictor and uncertainty signal. Appendix D likewise compares SCOPE with Trust-or-Escalate using a different confidence estimator and a different form of statistical certification. Applying each calibration procedure to the same BPE predictions and scores is needed to attribute coverage gains. The abstract's 'same risk constraint' comparison is also misleading when the compared naive method violates that constraint.

Originality is limited beyond the proposed guarantee. BPE combines established response swapping with probability averaging; binary entropy is a monotone transformation of max(p-bar, 1-p-bar), so it produces exactly the same selective ordering as averaged-probability confidence. The manuscript acknowledges borrowing the linear-expectation calibration approach. The empirical usefulness of this combination is plausible, but it does not compensate for the invalid central theorem. Moreover, permutation invariance establishes order invariance, not general freedom from preference biases.

Reproducibility has material ambiguities. Appendix B.3.2 extracts A/B logits at the first response token, while the prompt requires bracketed verdicts such as [[A]]; the manuscript does not explain conditioning on the bracket prefix or establish that these logits represent the actual verdict decision. Dataset versions, sampled instance identifiers, actual seeds, and executable implementation are not supplied. Appendix C's assertion of 2,000 JudgeBench instances also requires clarification of the source and any resampling.

Several interpretations overstate the reported results. Appendix C claims nearly universal calibration superiority, although verbalized confidence has lower ECE for both Qwen-14B extended-benchmark cases. Appendix G claims increasing coverage with calibration size, while Qwen-14B MT-Bench coverage decreases from 0.541 at n = 100 to 0.506 at n = 1,000. The label-noise experiment supports robustness to independent random flips, not the broader claim about realistic label imperfections. These issues reduce confidence in the discussion, especially where reliability and safe deployment are emphasized.

strengths: Significance: Reliable abstention for pairwise LLM judging is a useful problem. A lightweight method requiring two model evaluations and no retraining could benefit preference annotation and model evaluation.

Empirical merits: Table 1 reports consistent improvements over discrete Swap-and-Aggregate in ECE, AUROC, and AUPRC. Evaluation spans several judge sizes, additional benchmarks, and a specialized critic; the calibration-size, label-noise, and distribution-transfer experiments provide useful practical context.

Presentation and limitations: The basic pipeline is understandable, and the appendix supplies prompts, metric definitions, and inference settings. Section 6 appropriately acknowledges exchangeability, computational overhead, and logit-access requirements. Reporting transfer failures in Appendix H is valuable.
weaknesses: Soundness—decisive theoretical failure: Appendix A, Eq. 13 incorrectly equates expected test loss with the average calibration-plus-test loss evaluated at the calibration-fitted threshold. Symmetry within the calibration set does not establish symmetry between calibration and test observations. Theorem 2.1 is also directly false: let every example have the same uncertainty score, let errors be independent Bernoulli(0.2), and choose n=10 and alpha=0.1. Eq. 5 permits acceptance exactly when all ten calibration predictions are correct; otherwise the method abstains everywhere. Acceptance therefore has positive probability 0.8^10, but the independent test error conditional on acceptance remains 0.2. Thus E[ES]/E[S]=0.2>0.1 under IID sampling, contradicting the claimed guarantee. This invalidates the central certification claim, rather than merely leaving a proof detail unresolved.

Evaluation does not match the theorem's estimand: The theorem concerns a ratio of expectations over calibration and test randomness, whereas the experiments average per-split error fractions. These generally differ when coverage varies. The manuscript should report pooled errors divided by pooled selections and specify how zero-selection splits are handled. In the counterexample above, assigning zero risk to abstaining splits yields mean risk approximately 0.0215 despite the theorem's risk being 0.2. Consequently, curves below alpha do not establish the stated guarantee.

Comparative evidence is confounded: Table 3 gives the heuristic and naive methods predictive-probability scores, while SCOPE receives BPE and a different prediction rule. Appendix D likewise compares Trust-or-Escalate with discrete simulated-annotator confidence against SCOPE with continuous BPE. These comparisons cannot isolate the benefit of the calibration procedure. Applying competing calibration methods to identical BPE predictions and scores, with their guarantee strengths explicitly distinguished, is necessary to support the claimed coverage advantage.

Originality is limited beyond the unsupported guarantee: Bidirectional judging is established prior work, and BPE combines probability averaging with binary entropy. Entropy is a monotone transformation of max(p-bar, 1-p-bar), so it contributes no new ranking or threshold-selection capability beyond averaged-probability confidence. This can still be a useful empirical contribution, but the manuscript needs a sharper account of what is new relative to probability-level symmetrization and the cited linear-expectation framework.

Reproducibility has material ambiguities: Appendix B.3.2 extracts A/B logits at the first response-token position, but the prompt requests bracketed outputs such as [[A]]. Without specifying a forced prefix or verifying tokenization, it is unclear that these logits represent the actual verdict decision. Exact dataset versions, sampled example identifiers, sampling seeds, and separation of few-shot demonstrations from evaluation examples are also insufficiently specified.

Presentation and claim scope require correction: The abstract claims up to 2.4 times more accepted judgments than vanilla baselines, although vanilla has full coverage; the apparent comparison is with naive calibration. Section 4.2 claims improved coverage for larger MT-Bench judges, although Qwen-14B decreases from 0.566 to 0.504. Appendix H says transfer between similarly difficult benchmarks holds, although Arena-to-MT-Bench exceeds alpha for three judges. More broadly, permutation invariance does not establish general bias neutrality or fairness. There is no evident intrinsic ethical barrier to this research, but the impact statement's assurances of certified trustworthiness are unsupported by the current theory.

strengths: Significance: Selective pairwise judging addresses a useful practical problem: trading evaluation coverage against disagreement with reference preferences without retraining the judge.

Empirical contribution: Probability-level bidirectional aggregation shows consistent improvements over discrete Swap-and-Aggregate in Table 1. For example, Qwen-14B on MT-Bench improves AUROC from 0.679 to 0.777 and AUPRC from 0.851 to 0.932 while holding prediction accuracy fixed.

Evaluation breadth: The manuscript examines multiple model sizes, five benchmarks, a specialized critic, calibration-set size, label noise, and cross-benchmark transfer. These experiments provide useful evidence about the proposed uncertainty signal.

Presentation and limitations: The main pipeline is easy to follow, and the appendix supplies prompts, metric definitions, and infrastructure details. The discussion appropriately acknowledges exchangeability, logit access, and computational overhead; the transfer experiments help illustrate the distribution-shift limitation.
weaknesses: Soundness—decisive: Theorem 2.1 is false as stated. Consider independent examples with a constant uncertainty score, a fixed prediction, and independent error probability 0.20. Set n=10 and α=0.10. Equation 5 is feasible exactly when all ten calibration predictions are correct, an event of probability 0.8^10. On that event Equation 6 accepts every test example; otherwise it abstains. Consequently, E[ES]/E[S]=0.20, exceeding α despite independent, exchangeable data. This directly contradicts the central finite-sample guarantee.

Proof error: Appendix A, Equation 13, equates the expected test loss with the expected average calibration-plus-test loss at the same fitted threshold. Symmetry within the calibration set does not justify this equality: the threshold depends on calibration labels and treats the held-out test point differently. Swapping the test point into calibration generally changes the threshold. The bounded single-point correction does not repair this adaptive-selection issue.

Risk evaluation does not clearly match the theorem. Equation 7 concerns a ratio of expectations over calibration and test randomness, whereas the experiments report empirical accepted-set error averaged over splits. An average of per-split ratios generally differs from the ratio of aggregate errors to aggregate selections. The treatment of splits with no accepted predictions is also unspecified, which is particularly consequential for low-coverage settings such as JudgeBench. Report both estimands explicitly; favorable empirical averages cannot establish the claimed theorem.

Comparisons do not isolate the calibration contribution. Table 3 changes both the uncertainty/prediction mechanism and the calibration rule between Naïve and SCOPE. Table 7 likewise compares SCOPE+BPE against Trust-or-Escalate with discrete simulated-annotator confidence, without specifying the latter's confidence level or reporting its risk. Apply competing calibration methods to identical scores and predictions and distinguish marginal guarantees from high-probability guarantees before attributing coverage gains to SCOPE.

Originality and claim scope: BPE is a useful refinement of existing swap-and-aggregate procedures, but binary entropy is a monotone transformation of max(p̄,1−p̄), so it does not create a distinct selection ranking. The novelty lies principally in continuous probability aggregation and its empirical assessment. Permutation invariance also does not establish general bias neutrality: content, verbosity, and shared errors can survive both orderings. The manuscript repeatedly overstates this property.

Reproducibility: Appendix B.3.2 extracts A/B logits at the first response token, while the prompt requests [[A]] or [[B]]. It is unclear whether the opening brackets are supplied as a prefix or whether probabilities are taken before the actual verdict-token position. This distinction directly affects BPE. Exact dataset versions and sampled instance identifiers, split seeds, tie handling, and executable calibration code are also needed to reproduce and audit the results.

Presentation and significance claims exceed the reported evidence in several places. The abstract claims up to 2.4× coverage relative to vanilla under the same constraint, although vanilla has full coverage and does not satisfy that constraint; the 2.4× comparison corresponds to Naïve. Section 4.2 claims improvements for larger MT-Bench judges, although Qwen-14B coverage decreases from 0.566 to 0.504. The impact statement's claims of certified reliability should be revised following correction of the theorem. No separate material ethical violation is apparent, but unsupported certification is consequential for the proposed evaluation and supervision applications.
